tagline: More languages than any other country
overview:
Papua New Guinea occupies the eastern half of New Guinea, the world's second-largest island, along with hundreds of smaller islands in the southwest Pacific. It shares a land border with Indonesia and lies just north of Australia across the Torres Strait. At about 463,000 km² it is a little larger than Sweden.

About 10 million people live here, and they speak more than 800 languages, more than any other country on Earth. Tok Pisin, a creole that grew out of English and local languages, is the everyday shared tongue, along with English and Hiri Motu. Port Moresby is the capital.

Papua New Guinea is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament. Most people live in villages and grow their own food on small gardens of sweet potato, taro and bananas. The country holds gold, copper and gas, and some of the least explored rainforest and coral reef left in the world.
landAndNature: A rugged mountain spine runs the length of the island, rising above 4,500 meters at Mount Wilhelm, high enough for frost and once for small glaciers. Below the peaks lie deep valleys hidden from the outside world until the 1930s, then swamps, mighty rivers like the Sepik and Fly, and mangrove coasts. The country sits on the Ring of Fire, with active volcanoes such as Tavurvur, which buried the town of Rabaul in ash in 1994. New Guinea's wildlife is astonishing: about 40 species of birds-of-paradise perform dances with shimmering plumes, tree kangaroos climb in the canopy, the world's largest butterfly, Queen Alexandra's birdwing, has a wingspan of about 25 centimeters, and cassowaries stalk the forest floor.
peopleAndCulture: With hundreds of distinct peoples, Papua New Guinea holds some of the greatest cultural variety on Earth. At sing-sings, villages gather to dance in feathered headdresses, shell ornaments and painted faces, each group showing its own designs. Sepik River carvers make masks and spirit houses famous in museums worldwide. Food is cooked in a mumu, a pit lined with hot stones, and staples include sweet potato, sago, fish and pig, with pigs also serving as wealth and bride-price. Rugby league is a national passion, and the Kumuls draw huge crowds. Shell money is still used in some ceremonies. Most people follow Christianity blended with older traditions, and many clans still make decisions through big-man leaders and consensus.
history: People have lived in New Guinea for about 50,000 years, and farmers in the Kuk swamp were growing crops around 9,000 years ago, making it one of the places where agriculture was independently invented. The rugged terrain kept communities separate, which is why so many languages developed. European powers divided the island in the late 1800s: the Netherlands took the west, Germany the northeast and Britain the southeast, with Australia taking over the British part and, after World War I, the German part. Fierce fighting took place here in World War II, including the Kokoda Track campaign. Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia on September 16, 1975. A civil war on Bougainville island over a copper mine lasted from 1988 to 1998, and Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence in 2019.
funFacts: Papua New Guinea has over 800 living languages, roughly one in every nine languages spoken on Earth.
The Huli wigmen of the highlands grow their own hair into ceremonial wigs decorated with feathers and flowers.
Farmers in the Kuk swamp were draining land and growing crops around 9,000 years ago, among the world's earliest farmers.
Male birds-of-paradise clear a stage on the forest floor and dance upside down to impress females.
Tok Pisin words are wonderfully descriptive: a beard is 'mausgras', mouth grass, and a piano 'bikpela bokis'.
